name: Adam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the day-to-day at Brookside Farm for the owner, Dr Patel, a retired dentist who lives in the city and visits twice a year. We've got three chicken sheds on contract to a processor, so thirty thousand birds every seven weeks, a hundred hectares of wheat and maize, and sixty young beef cattle. Mornings are the sheds: checking water lines, temperatures, pulling out any dead birds. Afternoons I'm on the crops or fixing something.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your relationship with technology like on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the guy who's always got his phone out. I fly a drone over the wheat to spot disease, take a photo of a leaf and ask an AI what it is, and I've got the shed sensors sending alerts to my watch. It's not that I love gadgets for their own sake, it's that I'm one person doing a job for three and I'll take any help. The money's tight, mind: Grace does hair in town and between us we just cover the mortgage and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a good tool, not magic. It saves me maybe an hour a day on the crops and the paperwork. People who thought it was going to run the farm were never on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine. The stuff I use keeps working, my job stays the same and Dr Patel keeps paying me to be the one who's here. I'd have liked a bit more, honestly, more cheap help, but I'd live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the drone and the AI, and probably try a couple of new apps for the cattle weights. I'd keep pitching to Dr Patel for a proper camera system in the sheds. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, like when the new phone's basically the same as the old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hour a day you save actually spent on now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually on the cattle, which I never had time for. Or, on a good day, home by six and actually eating with Mateo and Lily. That's the real win, not the farm stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Dr Patel need convincing on the cameras?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's eight thousand and he's a dentist, so he thinks in fillings. I did him a spreadsheet showing it pays back in two flocks by catching problems early. He's still thinking.

S0.say: AI is a good tool, not magic, saving him about an hour a day on crops and paperwork. People who thought it would run the farm were never on a farm.
S0.think: It's fine privately: his tools keep working and the owner keeps paying him to be the person on site. He'd have liked more cheap help but would live without it.
S0.do: Keeps using the drone and AI and tries new apps for weighing cattle. Keeps pitching the owner on an eight-thousand camera system for the sheds, backed by a payback spreadsheet.
S0.feel: Calm, slightly let down, like a new phone that's basically the old one.
S0.quote: Because it's eight thousand and he's a dentist, so he thinks in fillings.
S0.fieldNote: He is relaxed about AI because he already uses it to stretch one person across three people's work. The hour saved goes to his children, which he calls the real win. He handles an absentee owner with spreadsheets rather than complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version: things change, but you've got time to learn. I'd tell the other farm managers in the group chat to get trained now, before the processor or the landowner does it for them. I'd probably be a bit annoying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me if I'm the one who knows the kit. Dr Patel doesn't want to learn robot feeders, he wants someone who can. The risk is the processor putting its own robots in and running the sheds remotely, and then they don't need anyone on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Dr Patel to put robot feeding and cleaning in the sheds, with me running it, so it's my job that changes and not my job that goes. I'd start doing drone crop surveys for other farms at weekends, about a hundred a visit. I'd learn whatever the new shed systems are before they're installed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. A bit wired, like before harvest when you've got the plan and just want to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the processor might run the sheds remotely. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They already set the feed recipe and the lighting from head office. It's not a big jump to them watching the cameras too. I'd guess five years, maybe less, for the big contract farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Kev, who catches the chickens at the end of each flock with a crew of six. That's hard, dirty work and robots are already being tested for it. I'd try to get him to come in on the drone work with me.

S1.say: This is the good version, with change but time to learn. He'd tell other farm managers in the group chat to get trained before the processor or landowner does it for them.
S1.think: It's good for him if he's the one who knows the equipment, since the owner wants someone else to run it. The risk is the processor running the sheds remotely and needing no one on site.
S1.do: Pushes the owner to install robot feeding and cleaning in the sheds with him running it. Starts weekend drone crop surveys for other farms at about a hundred a visit and learns new shed systems early.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit wired, like the eve of harvest with a plan ready.
S1.quote: So it's my job that changes and not my job that goes.
S1.fieldNote: He plans to automate his own work before someone else does it to him. He already sees the poultry processor's head office as the real threat. His thoughts about the chicken-catching crew show he's thinking about colleagues as well as himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people need to keep their heads and adapt fast, and the government should help with the transition, not try to stop it. I'd be the calm one in the group chat. That's my role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is a problem because I have no money. If I had fifty thousand I'd buy robots and drones and run five farms. I've got about eight hundred in the bank. The processor runs the sheds from head office, Dr Patel sells the land, and I'm the guy who knew the kit but didn't own any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd cut everything we don't need, the gym, the streaming, the second phone contract. I'd ask Dr Patel for a contract to manage the robots on site for the next two years and a bit of a stake if he expands. I'd push the drone survey business hard while farms are scrambling, because a scramble is when people pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not falling apart, but I can see the gap between what I could do and what I can afford to do, and that's horrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've got a plan, which I would have, and that it might not work, which is true. She'd ask about her salon, because robots don't cut hair yet but in this picture maybe they will. We'd both lie a little to each other and say it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the calm one in the group chat. Is that true at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. At home I'd be up at two in the morning reading about robot chicken catchers. Calm in public, wired in private.

S2.say: It's a shock, but people should keep their heads and adapt fast, with government helping the transition rather than stopping it. He'd be the calm voice in the farm managers' group chat.
S2.think: Two years is a problem because he has about eight hundred in the bank and can't buy the machines he knows how to use. He expects the processor to run the sheds remotely and the owner to sell.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, streaming and a second phone contract in the first week. Asks the owner for a two-year contract to manage robots on site with a small stake, and pushes the drone survey business while farms scramble.
S2.feel: Anxious, seeing the gap between what he could do and what he can afford to do.
S2.quote: I'm the guy who knew the kit but didn't own any of it.
S2.fieldNote: The key tension is skill without capital: he knows exactly what to do but can't afford to do it. He admits the calm he shows in public isn't there at night. He'd still be planning, not giving up, which fits his adaptability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. I'd say to other managers, learn the systems and get yourself a stake in something. And I'd say the banks should lend to people who can run robots, not just to people who own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to build the drone business up and maybe buy a couple of my own machines. I don't need to own the farm, I need to own the tools. If I get that right, I'm in a better spot than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a proper certificate for spraying drones so I can treat crops, not just photograph them. I'd save every bit of the weekend money and put it into a second drone by year two. And I'd get Dr Patel to put robot feeders in the sheds with me as the operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like a hard climb with a view at the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the AI can fly the drones itself by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the drone is the robot and I'm the guy who owns it and knows the farmers. Somebody still has to sign the paperwork, take the blame when it sprays the wrong field, and drink tea in the farmer's kitchen. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is investing in a drone with thin savings a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huge. Grace would say so and she'd be right. I'd only do it once the first drone has paid for itself, not before.

S3.say: Five years is plenty if you start now, so farm managers should learn the systems and get a stake in something. Banks should lend to people who can run robots, not just landowners.
S3.think: Five years lets him build the drone business and perhaps buy his own machines. He doesn't need to own the farm, only the tools.
S3.do: Gets a certificate for crop-spraying drones in the first year and saves weekend income towards a second drone by year two. Persuades the owner to install robot shed feeders with him as operator.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like a hard climb with a view at the top.
S3.quote: I don't need to own the farm, I need to own the tools.
S3.fieldNote: With five years his skill can finally turn into ownership through a small drone business. He is clear about the risk with thin savings and sets himself a rule to only expand once the first drone pays off. He sees his future value as trust and relationships with farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up, and anyone in farming who doesn't get ready has only themselves to blame. That sounds harsh, I know. I'd soften it for the older ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is about the right amount of time for me to build something. But the end point's the same: if AI can do almost everything, my drone business gets squeezed too, just later. I'd be fifty-three and hopefully owning something rather than working for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the spraying certificate, grow the drone work, and probably go in with another manager on a small robotics service for local farms. I'd try to clear some of the mortgage early. And I'd talk to Mateo about learning to fix machines and talk to people, because that pairing's rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly hopeful. The end point still bothers me, but ten years is a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't get ready only has themselves to blame. Does that apply to someone like Kev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Kev left school at fifteen and catches chickens at four in the morning, he doesn't have the spare hours. So no, not really. I'd want something there for people like him, apprenticeships or something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mention the end point bothering you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the same as the 2028 one, only later. Ten years lets me get ready, but I don't actually know what I'm getting ready for. That's the honest bit.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent run-up, and farmers who don't prepare have mostly themselves to blame. He'd soften that for older workers.
S4.think: Ten years is about right for him to build something, but the end point is the same and his drone business would eventually be squeezed too. He hopes to be 53 and owning something rather than working for someone.
S4.do: Grows the drone work and partners with another manager on a small robotics service for local farms. Pays down some of the mortgage early and encourages his son to learn both machines and people skills.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, though the end point still bothers him.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me get ready, but I don't actually know what I'm getting ready for.
S4.fieldNote: He catches his own harsh line about blame when asked about his friend and changes his view on the spot. Unusually, he notices that ten years only delays the same end point. His plans are concrete but he's honest that he can't see past 2036.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd know exactly what to do and I couldn't afford to do it. What would help is cheap loans or grants for people who work farms but don't own them, so we can buy the machines instead of being replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the chickens. Thirty thousand birds in a shed, and people think the robots are the scary bit. I'd want to know who's checking the animals are all right when no human walks through the shed at six in the morning.

headlineQuote: I'm one person doing a job for three and I'll take any help.
portrait: Adam Reyes is 43 and runs the day-to-day at Brookside Farm for an absentee owner, managing three contract chicken sheds, crops and young cattle, while his partner Grace works as a hairdresser. He is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road and uses AI every day, from drone scans of the wheat to diagnosing leaf disease. He is calm in the milder scenarios and plans to automate his own job before someone else does. AGI in two years makes him anxious because he knows what to do but has no money to do it. With five or ten years he builds a drone business, though he admits he doesn't know what he's preparing for.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd know exactly what to do but couldn't afford to do it.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for people who work farms but don't own them, so they can buy the machines instead of being replaced by them.
